blocks.prompt: The Snake That Smells With Its Tongue
blocks.text: A snake has no legs, but it is never stuck. It slides over sand. It climbs trees. Some snakes even swim. A snake moves by pushing its body into curves. The wide scales on its belly grip the ground and pull it along. A snake does not have eyelids. It cannot blink or shut its eyes. A clear scale sits over each eye like a tiny window. When a snake grows too big for its skin, it crawls out of the old one and leaves it behind. The new skin is already there, shiny and ready.

blocks.prompt: How a Snake Smells the Air
blocks.text: A snake's tongue is not for tasting food. It is for smelling. Watch a snake move through the grass. Its tongue flicks out, touches the air, and darts back in. Tiny bits of scent stick to the wet tongue. Back inside the mouth, the snake presses those bits against a special patch in the roof of its mouth called the Jacobson's organ. That patch reads the scent and tells the snake what is nearby. Here is the clever part. A snake's tongue is forked, with two thin points. Each point picks up its own sample of air. If the left point brings back more mouse smell than the right point, the mouse is off to the left. The snake does not just smell the air. It smells which direction the smell is coming from. You do something like this with your ears. Two ears let you hear which way a sound came from. A snake has two tongue tips instead, and it follows a scent trail the way you might follow a sound.

notes: The lower jaw is two bones, not one
The quadrate bone acts as an extra hinge

Snakes cannot chew at all

blocks.prompt: The Mouth That Opens Wider Than the Head
blocks.text: A snake cannot chew. It has no flat teeth for grinding and no hands for tearing. Whatever a snake eats, it eats whole, and it often eats animals much wider than its own head. People say a snake unhinges its jaw. That is not quite right, and the truth is stranger. Your lower jaw is one solid bone, fused at your chin. A snake's lower jaw is two separate bones, joined at the front only by a stretchy ligament. Those two halves can spread apart sideways and slide forward and back on their own. Behind them sits a small bone called the quadrate, which works like an extra elbow between the skull and the jaw, swinging the whole mouth open far wider than a fused skull ever could. Swallowing is not a gulp. It is a walk. The snake hooks the curved teeth on one side of its mouth into the meal, pulls, then releases that side and hooks the other side further along. Left, right, left, right, the snake slowly walks its own head over the food. While all that is happening, the snake still has to breathe. A tube at the bottom of its mouth, the glottis, pushes forward past the meal like a snorkel and keeps the air moving. A meal that takes an hour to swallow does not suffocate the animal swallowing it.

notes: Pit organs read infrared heat
The membrane is thin as tissue paper
It can register thousandths of a degree
Heat and sight merge in the brain
Rattlesnakes, pythons and boas all have pits
Around 4,000 snake species are alive today

blocks.prompt: Seeing Heat in Total Darkness
blocks.text: Put a pit viper in a room with no light at all, and it will still find the mouse. Along the upper lip of a rattlesnake, and in a row of small openings on the face of a python or a boa, sit organs no other animal quite matches. Each pit is a shallow cup with a membrane stretched across the middle of it, thin as tissue paper and packed with nerve endings. Warm objects give off infrared radiation, and infrared is nothing more than light too red for your eyes to see. The membrane absorbs it, warms very slightly, and the nerves report the temperature change. A pit viper's membrane can register a difference of a few thousandths of a degree. Here is what makes it more than a thermometer. The pit has an opening at the front, and the membrane sits behind it, which is the same arrangement as a pinhole camera. Heat arriving from the left of the snake lands on the right of the membrane. That means the organ does not just announce that something warm exists. It reports where. With two pits, one on each side of the head, the snake gets overlapping fields and can judge distance, the same way your two eyes do. The signals travel to a part of the brain that also handles vision, and there they merge with what the eyes are already reporting. Biologists suspect the snake does not experience heat and sight as two separate senses at all, but as one picture with the warm parts glowing inside it. The pits evolved twice. Pit vipers built theirs into a deep hollow between the eye and the nostril, while pythons and boas built rows of shallower ones into the scales of the lip. The structures are not the same, and the two groups are not close relatives. Yet both landed on the same molecule to do the sensing, a protein in the nerve endings that changes shape when it warms. Two separate lineages, working on the same problem, reached for the same tool. The result is a hunter that works at night, aims at the warmest part of an animal, and strikes accurately at prey it has never seen.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Snakes sit inside the lizard family tree
Najash: a 95 million year old snake with hind legs
Pythons still carry vestigial leg spurs
The ZRS limb switch is broken in snakes
The left lung is reduced or absent
About 4,000 species, on every continent but Antarctica

blocks.prompt: The Body That Gave Up Its Legs
blocks.text: A snake is a lizard. Not like a lizard, not descended from something that also happened to produce lizards. A snake sits inside the lizard family tree the way a bat sits inside the mammal family tree, and almost everything strange about a snake is what happened to a lizard that stopped using its legs. The fossils are clear about the order of events. Najash rionegrina, dug out of 95 million year old rock in Argentina, was a snake with a snake's skull and a long snake's body, and it still had small hind legs and a hip to hang them from. Other early snakes from the same period carried the same shrunken back limbs. Legs did not vanish in one step. They were kept, then reduced, then abandoned, and pythons and boas have not entirely finished the process. Under the skin near the tail, a python still carries two tiny leg bones and a claw-shaped spur on each side, useless for walking. Biologists can now point at the switch. A stretch of DNA called the ZRS does not build limbs itself. It is a control panel that tells the limb-building gene when and where to fire. In snakes, that control panel has crumbled. In 2016, researchers took the broken python version and put it into mice in place of the working mouse copy. The mice grew stumps. Losing legs was only the beginning. What followed was a redesign of nearly everything. A lizard's spine is divided into regions: neck, chest, hips, tail. Snakes flattened that plan and repeated one section over and over, so a python may carry more than four hundred vertebrae, each with its own pair of ribs. A body that long has no room for a body's usual layout. Paired organs could not sit side by side, so they were staggered front to back, one kidney ahead of the other. The left lung shrank to a scrap or vanished entirely, and the right lung stretched down the animal like a long balloon. The senses were rebuilt too. Snake eyes are not lizard eyes made smaller. They are put together differently, focusing by sliding the lens forward and back like a camera rather than squeezing it into a new shape, which is the sort of thing that happens when a lineage loses good vision underground and then has to invent it again on the way back out. The ears went the other way. A snake has no eardrum and no ear opening. Sound reaches the inner ear through the jawbone, which rests against the ground, so a snake hears the world mostly by leaning on it. Against the losses, count what was gained. A forked tongue that samples the air in stereo. A lower jaw split into two halves that walk a meal down the throat. In some lineages, pits on the face that read body heat as an image. None of that was possible on the old lizard body plan. The score is worth noticing. There are around four thousand species of snake, on every continent but Antarctica, in deserts, rivers, treetops, and open ocean. An animal that threw away its limbs did not become a lesser lizard. It became a different solution, and by most measures a spectacularly successful one.
